Degradation products were identified and quantified to probe reaction pathways at different pH values, highlighting the role of radical speciation in PFOA breakdown.

evidence_passages.passage: The work evaluates non‑thermal plasma at atmospheric pressure (APPJ) for treating PFAS‑contaminated water in several matrices, achieving successful removal of C4–C6 PFCAs, C4–C8 PFSAs, and perfluoropolyethers GenX and ADONA in laboratory‑scale experiments.

Matrix effects were shown to influence degradation rates, and by‑product analysis indicated different mechanisms for PFSAs/PFCAs versus ether‑containing PFPEs, informing technology selection for emerging PFAS.

source_limitations: Preprint; peer review pending.
Details on operating conditions, kinetics and energy use are not fully available from the abstract page.

source.citation: Tang C. et al., Hinkley Center for PFAS, Final Project Report, 2022.

evidence_passages.passage: A thin‑film non‑thermal plasma gas–liquid reactor treated three real municipal solid waste landfill leachates and synthetic waters containing PFOA and other PFAS.

Of 21 PFAS above quantification limits in the leachates, 17 were removed; PFOA removals were 76%, 65% and 89% for three leachates, while several short‑chain PFAS (e.g., PFBA, FBSA) increased as daughter products.

Sodium chloride at near‑seawater concentration significantly decreased energy efficiency, whereas other leachate components (acetate, humic acids, surfactants, pH) reduced PFOA mineralization by less than 30%.
The reactor uses nanosecond pulses (16 kV, 40 ns, 5 kHz) in a small tubular geometry with argon gas and a liquid flow of 2 mL min−1, giving a hydraulic residence time of about 0.2 s.

source_limitations: Technical report; some methods and QA/QC details may differ from journal standards.
Leachate chemistry is site‑specific; transferability to other leachates requires caution.
Energy metrics are discussed but not comprehensively benchmarked against alternatives.
source.title: Non-thermal plasma degradation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in landfill leachate using a thin-film gas-liquid reactor

source.citation: Lin J.-C. et al., Ultrasonics Sonochemistry, 2015, 22, 542–547.

evidence_passages.passage: The study examined PFOA decomposition by ultrasonic irradiation at various pH, sulfate concentrations, powers and temperatures, finding almost complete decomposition within 90 min at 25 °C and 117 mM sulfate.
The decomposition followed pseudo‑first‑order kinetics and was attributed to both direct cavitation and sulfate radical attack in the sulfate‑assisted sonochemical system.

source_limitations: Single‑compound PFOA solutions; no competing co‑contaminants or salinity typical of real wastewaters.
Reactor geometry is not fully described on the abstract page.
Energy consumption is not explicitly quantified in kWh m−3.

evidence_passages.passage: The study investigated ultrasonic degradation of PFOA, PFOS and 6:2 FTS across 580–1144 kHz, 125–187.5 W, 0.08–40 ppm initial PFAS, and 0.5–3 h treatment, including real AFFF and foam‑fractionate wastes.

Optimised conditions achieved around 125% defluorination in AFFF waste and 115% in foam fractionate relative to TOP‑assay fluorine, while PFAS removal reached about 65% and 97% respectively, indicating intermediate generation.

source_limitations: Abstract‑level view only; detailed reactor geometry and hydrodynamics are not visible.
Energy consumption and cost are not directly reported in the inspected text.
Study is still bench‑scale; translation to full‑scale systems is not resolved.

source.citation: Khoshyan A. et al., Journal of Water Process Engineering, 2024, 63, 105511.

evidence_passages.passage: Using indirect ultrasonication at 130 kHz and 100% effective power for 3 h, approximately 95% and 46% defluorination of PFOA were obtained in glass and polypropylene reactors, respectively.

Similar trends in reactor-material dependence were observed for PFOS, 6:2 FTS and an AFFF mixture, with glass reactors showing higher ultrasonic energy transfer efficiency and faster PFAS degradation kinetics.

The mechanism analysis suggested a primary pyrolytic pathway inside cavitation bubbles, with hydroxyl radicals providing a secondary contribution confirmed via KI dosimetry and benzoic acid scavenging.

source_limitations: Laboratory‑scale indirect ultrasonication; no continuous‑flow reactor evaluated.
Study focuses on reactor materials; effects of salinity and co‑contaminants are limited.
Energy use is expressed as W L−1 and duration; cost translation is not provided.

source.citation: Niu J.F. et al., Journal of Environmental Sciences, 2019.

evidence_passages.passage: Trace‑level PFOS and PFOA were treated in water using a 20 kHz probe‑type sonicator at ultrasound power between 150 and 375 W, achieving complete removal within about 80 min under optimal conditions.
Pseudo‑first‑order kinetics and mechanistic pathways were derived as functions of initial concentration, power level, solution pH and temperature, providing a kinetic basis for sonolysis design.

source_limitations: Abstract only; reactor geometry and volume specifics are not visible.

evidence_passages.passage: An autocatalytic permanganate–ultrasonic (PM–US) system was applied to degrade PFOA in aqueous solution, combining chemical oxidant with sonolysis to enhance degradation.
The hybrid system enabled higher PFOA removal and defluorination than ultrasound or permanganate alone, indicating synergistic oxidative and cavitational pathways.

source_limitations: Single‑compound PFOA system; does not represent complex PFAS mixtures or real wastewaters.
Co‑contaminant and salinity effects are not addressed.

evidence_chunks.text: Electrochemical degradation using boron-doped diamond (BDD) electrodes was applied to PFAS-contaminated water and wastewater, achieving up to 99.5% PFOA removal and about 50% fluoride release under optimized conditions.

The study evaluated PFOA and other PFAS in spiked water and municipal wastewater, using a flow-through BDD reactor and varying current density, electrolyte conductivity and supporting electrolyte composition.
Up to 56% of total PFAS were degraded in real wastewaters under best-performing conditions determined in synthetic solutions, highlighting matrix interferences and incomplete mineralization.
Energy consumption was reported in kWh m−3 and depended strongly on current density and organic loading; higher currents increased removal but also specific energy demand.

source_limitations: Bench-scale experiments only; no pilot/field deployment.
Primarily treats relatively simple PFAS mixtures in laboratory and municipal wastewater.
Energy metrics and cost are reported but not optimized for scale-up.

evidence_chunks.text: A boron‑doped graphene sponge anode was synthesized and applied for electrochemical oxidation of C4–C8 PFAS in a one‑pass flow‑through mode at 230 A m−2, with removal efficiencies from about 17% to 67%.
Specific energy consumption for these flow‑through experiments was approximately 10 kWh m−3, and removal was partitioned between electrosorption and electrooxidation based on fluorine mass balance.
The anode showed negligible chlorate and perchlorate formation even in brackish solutions, suggesting advantages for high‑salinity PFAS-rich brines and ion‑exchange regenerates.

source_limitations: Preprint; not yet peer‑reviewed.
Experiments are bench‑scale with synthetic electrolyte and relatively simple PFAS mixtures.
Long‑term stability, fouling, and cost of graphene sponge electrodes are not fully resolved.

Maximum degradation of about 90% for PFOA and 96% for PFOS was achieved at an optimal 2 kHz repetition frequency at sub‑µg L−1 influent concentrations.
The reactor is a gas–liquid flowing film configuration where plasma channels propagate along the gas–liquid interface, exploiting PFAS surface activity to concentrate them at the reaction zone.
